# Group 13 Assignment 7

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# rm(list = ls()) # un-comment this for first run of script

library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("ggrepel")

options(bitmapType = "cairo")

raw_dir <- "../data/_raw/"
data_file <- "gravier.RData"
data_loc <- "https://github.com/ramhiser/datamicroarray/raw/master/data/"

# Allow R to create nested directories
if( !dir.exists(raw_dir) ){
  dir.create(path = raw_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

# Download file
if( !file.exists(str_c(raw_dir, data_file)) ){
  download.file(
    url = str_c(data_loc, data_file),
    destfile = str_c(raw_dir, data_file)
  )
}

# Load the data
load(file = str_c(raw_dir, data_file))
```

## Creating tidy data

Working with data can be can be difficult, especially because everyone does it differently. Tidy data solves this problem. A "tidy" data set is defined by:

1.  Every variable must have its own column
2.  Every observation must have its own row
3.  Every variable must have its own cell

By integrating these rules, data becomes much simpler and easier to work with.

### Wrangling the data

For this assignment, we will be working with the gravier data set, which examines metastasis for breast cancer. You will see below, how the data is wrangled to become tidy, with additional calculations for later analysis.

#### Data Wrangling

```{r}
gravier_clean <- gravier |>
  bind_cols() |>
  as_tibble()


gravier_clean_aug <- gravier_clean |> 
  mutate(y = case_when(y == "poor" ~ 1,
                       y == "good" ~ 0)) |> 
  relocate(early_metastasis = y)


# Making the data tidy
# -------------------------------------------------

gravier_clean_aug_long <- gravier_clean_aug |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -early_metastasis,
               names_to = "Gene",
               values_to = "log2_expr_level")

# -------------------------------------------------


gravier_clean_aug_long_nested <- gravier_clean_aug_long |> 
  group_by(Gene) |> 
  nest() |> 
  mutate(model_object = map(.x = data,
                   .f = ~lm(formula = log2_expr_level ~ early_metastasis,
                            data = .x))) |> 
  ungroup()

gravier_clean_aug_long_nested <-  gravier_clean_aug_long_nested |> 
  mutate(model_object_tidy = map(.x = model_object,
                                 .f = ~pluck(.x) |> 
                                   tidy(conf.int = TRUE,
                                        conf.level = 0.95),
                                 data = .x))

gravier_estimates <- gravier_clean_aug_long_nested |> 
  unnest(model_object_tidy) |> 
  filter(term == "early_metastasis") |> 
  select(c("Gene", "p.value", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")) |> 
  mutate("q.value" = p.adjust(`p.value`),
         "is_significant" = case_when(`q.value` < 0.05 ~ "yes",
                                      `q.value` >= 0.05 ~ "no")) |> 
  ungroup()
```

In the chunk above, the original data frame is pivoted to be long, creating the tidy data set that we want. By doing this, the data goes from this:

```{r}
gravier_clean_aug %>% 
  slice_sample(n = 10)
```

After using the function pivot_longer (outlined in the chunk above), the data is now tidy, and looks like this:

```{r}
gravier_clean_aug_long %>% 
  slice_sample(n=10)
```

At this point, the rules for a tidy data set is met, and further analysis can be done.

## **Analysis Question**

Having finalized the data wrangling, we are now ready to investigate which of the genes have been up- and down-regulated in patients with clinical signs of early metastasis.

The column which is added last while preparing the data, called `is_significant,` allow us to distinguish between the genes whose expression have changed significantly, according to a threshold value of $\alpha = 0.05$. This allow us to display only those genes of all 2905, that are significantly regulated, e.g. in a forest plot as seen below, where we display the $log_2(expression)$ of each gene with a corresponding 95% confidence interval (95% CIs). This shows qualitatively, how these 43 genes differ from each other, without overwhelming the viewer with the remaining 2862 observations. The volcano plot that is seen further below gives an overview of the overall distribution of the expression of all genes.

In addition to the plot that was produced last week, we have added a color scaling to the data points, which enables a deciphering of any tendencies in how the significance is distributed.

```{r}
no_sig <- gravier_estimates |> 
  filter(is_significant == "yes") |> 
  count() |> 
  pull()
no_sig

count(gravier_estimates) |> pull() - no_sig
```

```{r}
gravier_estimates |> 
  filter(is_significant == "yes") |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = estimate, 
        y = fct_reorder(Gene, estimate))) +
  
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = `conf.low`, 
        xmax = `conf.high`), alpha = 0.3) +  
  
  geom_point(aes(color = p.value)) + 
  
  xlim(-0.3,0.3) +
  
  scale_colour_viridis_c("p-value", option = "plasma", direction = 1) +

  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey") +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  
  labs(y = "Genes",
       x = "Estimates (95% CIs)",
       title = "Genes Associated with Early Metastasis \nin Small Node-Negative Breast Carcinoma",
       caption = "Data from DOI: 10.1002/gcc.20820") +
  
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5), 
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 5),
        legend.title.align = 0.5,
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## **What genes are significantly up- or down-regulated between the patients with/without early metastasis?**

Several genes are significantly up- and down-regulated in patients with early metastasis as seen in both the forest plot as well as the volcano plot. The genes g1CNS507 and g1CNS91 are the most up- and down regulated genes respectively and therefore have a highly significant effect on early metastasis of breast cancer. Increased risk of early metastasis of small node-negative breast carcinoma is implied by the data in a significant down-regulation of the gene g1CNS507. However, the uncertainties are quite large for most of the significant genes as seen in the forest plot which urges the reader to not define which gene hold the single most weight in the analysis. A complete list of the significant genes can be seen below:

```{r}
gravier_estimates |>
  filter(is_significant == "yes")|>
  pull(Gene)
```

## Volcano-plot analysis of significantly regulated genes

```{r}
gravier_estimates |> 
  
  
  ggplot(
    aes(x=estimate, 
        y = -log10(`p.value`), 
        
        # creating colour coding and matching labels for signif genes
        colour = ifelse(is_significant == "no", "blue", "red"), 
        label = ifelse(is_significant == "yes", Gene, ""))) +
  
  # visualize via scatter plot
  geom_point(show.legend = F,
             alpha = 0.5, 
             size = 1) +
  
  # add labels to signif genes
  geom_text_repel(size = 2, 
                  show.legend = F, 
                  max.overlaps = 20) +
  
  # add a horizontal line for y=0
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  
  labs(y = "-log10(p)",
       x = "Estimates",
       title = "Genes Associated with Early Metastasis in Small Node-Negative Breast Carcinoma",
       caption = "Data from DOI: 10.1002/gcc.20820",
       subtitle = "Genes highlighted in turquoise were significant after multiple testing correction") +
  
  # centre plot title and subtitle
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 1),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 1))
```
